arXiv:2011.10304v2 [math.AP] 12 Nov 2021

Evolution of dietary diversity and a starvation driven cross-diffusion system as its singular limit

E. Brocchieri    L. Corrias    H. Dietert    Y.-J. Kim
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We rigorously prove the passage from a Lotka-Volterra reaction-diffusion system towards a cross-diffusion system at the fast reaction limit. The system models a competition of two species, where one species has a more diverse diet than the other. The resulting limit gives a cross-diffusion system of a starvation driven type. We investigate the linear stability of homogeneous equilibria of those systems and rule out the possibility of cross-diffusion induced instability (Turing instability). Numerical simulations are included which are compatible with the theoretical results.

Keywords. Cross-diffusion, starvation-driven diffusion, entropy, Turing instability.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary : 35B25, 35B40, 35K57, 35Q92, 92D25. Secondary 35B45, 35K45

1 Introduction

1.1 Problem setting

We consider a semilinear reaction-diffusion system that models a competition dynamics when two species have partially different diets. The population densities of the two species are denoted by u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) and v=v⁡(t,x)v=v(t,x). The species uu has a more diverse diet and is divided into two substates ua=ua​(t,x)u_{a}=u_{a}(t,x) and ub=ub​(t,x)u_{b}=u_{b}(t,x) so that u=ua+ubu=u_{a}+u_{b}. The system is parametrized by a small parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0 and written as

{∂tuaε=daΔuaε+fa(uaε)+1εQ(uaε,ubε,vε),in⁡(0,+∞)×Ω,∂tubε=db​Δ​ubε+fb​(ubε,vε)−1ε​Q​(uaε,ubε,vε),in⁡(0,+∞)×Ω,∂tvε=dv​Δ​vε+fv​(ubε,vε),in⁡(0,+∞)×Ω,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u_{a}^{\varepsilon}=d_{a}\Delta u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+f_{a}(u_{a}^{\varepsilon})+\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}Q(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},\,u_{b}^{\varepsilon},\,v^{\varepsilon}\,),\hskip 18.49988pt&\In\,\,(0,+\infty)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}u_{b}^{\varepsilon}=d_{b}\Delta u_{b}^{\varepsilon}+f_{b}(u_{b}^{\varepsilon},\,v^{\varepsilon})-\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}Q(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},\,u_{b}^{\varepsilon},\,v^{\varepsilon}\,),&\In\,\,(0,+\infty)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v^{\varepsilon}=d_{v}\Delta v^{\varepsilon}+f_{v}(u_{b}^{\varepsilon},\,v^{\varepsilon}),&\In\,\,(0,+\infty)\times\Omega,\end{cases} (1.1)

where Ω⊂ℝN\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{N}}, N≥1\mathrm{N}\geq 1, is a bounded domain with a smooth boundary, and da,dbd_{a},d_{b} and dvd_{v} are diffusivities for the three populations. The unknown solutions depend on the parameter ε\varepsilon and we denote it explicitly if needed. The above system is complemented with nonnegative initial data

uaε​(0,x)=uain​(x),ubε​(0,x)=ubin​(x),vε​(0,x)=vin​(x),x∈Ω,u_{a}^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=u_{a}^{\text{in}}(x)\,,\hskip 9.24994ptu_{b}^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=u_{b}^{\text{in}}(x)\,,\hskip 9.24994ptv^{\varepsilon}(0,x)=v^{\text{in}}(x)\,,\hskip 9.24994ptx\in\Omega\,, (1.2)

and zero flux boundary conditions,

da∇uaε⋅σ=db∇ubε⋅σ=dv∇vε⋅σ=0,on (0,+∞)×∂Ω,d_{a}\nabla u_{a}^{\varepsilon}\cdot\sigma=d_{b}\nabla u_{b}^{\varepsilon}\cdot\sigma=d_{v}\nabla v^{\varepsilon}\cdot\sigma=0\hskip 2.84544pt,\hskip 9.24994pt\text{on }(0,+\infty)\times\,\partial\Omega\,, (1.3)

where σ\sigma denotes the outward unit normal vector on the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

In this paper, we explore the effect of diet diversity in a competition context and show the emergence of cross-diffusion triggered by the different substates uau_{a} and ubu_{b}, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. The competition dynamics is given in the reaction terms. The reaction terms of order one are given by

fa​(ua)\displaystyle f_{a}(u_{a}) :=ηa​ua​(1−uaa),\displaystyle:=\eta_{a}u_{a}\Big(1-\dfrac{u_{a}}{a}\Big),
fb​(ub,v)\displaystyle f_{b}(u_{b},v) :=ηb​ub​(1−ub+vb),\displaystyle:=\eta_{b}u_{b}\Big(1-\dfrac{u_{b}+v}{b}\Big), (1.4)
fv​(ub,v)\displaystyle f_{v}(u_{b},v) :=ηv​v​(1−ub+vb),\displaystyle:=\eta_{v}v\Big(1-\dfrac{u_{b}+v}{b}\Big)\,,

where a,b>0a,b>0 are carrying capacities supported by two different groups of resources and ηa,ηb\eta_{a},\eta_{b}, and ηv>0\eta_{v}>0 are the intrinsic growth rates of ua,ubu_{a},u_{b}, and vv, respectively. The competition of the two species, uu and vv, is for the resource bb. However, the species uu has a diverse diet and can survive by consuming the other resource aa without competition. To model such a competition using a Lotka-Volterra type system, the species uu is divided into two substates uau_{a} and ubu_{b} depending on their diets. In the above reaction terms, uau_{a} takes a logistic equation type reaction, and ubu_{b} and vv take Lotka-Volterra competition equations type reactions as given in (1.4). Since competition exists only partially for the species uu, the competition is weak for uu. However, the species vv competes with uu for all of its resources and hence the competition is not weak in general and the competition result may depend on the parameter ε\varepsilon (see Sections 4 and 5).

The individuals of the species uu may freely change the type of food depending on the availability, which is modelled by the fast reaction term of order ε−1\varepsilon^{-1},

1ε​Q​(ua,ub,v):=1ε​[ϕ⁡(ub+vb)​ub−ψ⁡(uaa)​ua],ε>0.\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,Q(u_{a},u_{b},v):=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,\bigg[\phi\Big(\dfrac{u_{b}+v}{b}\Big)\,u_{b}-\psi\Big(\dfrac{u_{a}}{a}\Big)\,u_{a}\,\bigg]\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\varepsilon>0\,. (1.5)

In this reaction term, ϵ−1​ϕ​(ub+vb)\epsilon^{-1}\,\phi\Big(\dfrac{u_{b}+v}{b}\Big) is the conversion rate for individuals in the state ubu_{b} which switch to the other state uau_{a}, and ϵ−1​ψ​(uaa)\epsilon^{-1}\,\psi\Big(\dfrac{u_{a}}{a}\Big) is the conversion rate in the other direction. The conversion rate ϕ⁡(ub+vb)\phi\big(\frac{u_{b}+v}{b}\big) is assumed as a function of the starvation measure ub+vb\frac{u_{b}+v}{b} for the populations ubu_{b} and vv. If the resource bb dwindles or the population ub+vu_{b}+v increases, the resource bb becomes scarce relatively, and more individuals of population ubu_{b} will convert to uau_{a} and consume the other resource aa. Hence, we assume that ϕ\phi is an increasing function of the starvation measure (see [22] for more discussion on the starvation measure). In the same way, the conversion rate ψ\psi is a function of the starvation measure uaa\frac{u_{a}}{a} for the population uau_{a} and is assumed to be increasing. For this reason, it makes sense to call the conversion dynamics given by (1.5) a starvation-driven conversion, which eventually results in the starvation-driven cross-diffusion after taking the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 (see [8, 9]). More specifically, we assume the following starvation-driven conversion hypothesis

  • (H1)

    ϕ\phi and ψ\psi in (1.5) are increasing functions belonging to C1([0,+∞))C^{1}([0,+\infty)); in addition, there exist strictly positive constants δψ\delta_{\psi}, δϕ\delta_{\phi}, Mϕ′M_{\phi^{\prime}}, and Mψ′M_{\psi^{\prime}} such that, for all x≥0x\geq 0,

    ψ⁡(x)≥δψ>0,ϕ⁡(x)≥δϕ>0,ϕ′​(x)≤Mϕ′,and​ψ′​(x)≤Mψ′.\psi(x)\geq\delta_{\psi}>0,\hskip 9.24994pt\phi(x)\geq\delta_{\phi}>0,\hskip 9.24994pt\phi^{\prime}(x)\leq M_{\phi^{\prime}},\hskip 9.24994pt\text{and}\hskip 9.24994pt\psi^{\prime}(x)\leq M_{\psi^{\prime}}.

The main result of the paper is that, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the (unique) solution (uaε,ubε,vε)(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) of the initial boundary value problem (1.1)–(1.5) converges to a limit (ua,ub,v)(u_{a},u_{b},v) and this limit is a weak solution of the reaction cross-diffusion system

{∂tu=Δ⁡(da​ua+db​ub)+fa​(ua)+fb​(ub,v),in⁡(0,+∞)×Ω,∂tv=dv​Δ​v+fv​(ub,v),in⁡(0,+∞)×Ω,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta(d_{a}u_{a}+d_{b}u_{b})+f_{a}(u_{a})+f_{b}(u_{b},v),\hskip 9.24994pt&\In\,\,(0,+\infty)\times\Omega,\\ \partial_{t}v=d_{v}\Delta v+f_{v}(u_{b},v),&\In\,\,(0,+\infty)\times\Omega,\end{cases} (1.6)

where uau_{a} and ubu_{b} are (uniquely) determined by the nonlinear system

ua+ub=u​and​Q​(ua,ub,v)=0,u_{a}+u_{b}=u\hskip 9.24994pt\text{and}\hskip 9.24994ptQ(u_{a},u_{b},v)=0, (1.7)

complemented by the initial data,

u⁡(0,x)=uin​(x):=uain​(x)+ubin​(x),v⁡(0,x)=vin​(x),x∈Ω,u(0,x)=u^{\text{in}}(x):=u_{a}^{\text{in}}(x)+u_{b}^{\text{in}}(x)\,,\hskip 9.24994ptv(0,x)=v^{\text{in}}(x)\,,\hskip 9.24994ptx\in\Omega\,, (1.8)

and the zero flux boundary condition,

∇(daua+dbub)⋅σ=dv∇v⋅σ=0,in(0,+∞)×∂Ω.\nabla(d_{a}u_{a}+d_{b}u_{b})\cdot\sigma=d_{v}\nabla v\cdot\sigma=0\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\In\,\,(0,+\infty)\times\partial\Omega\,. (1.9)

Note that the zero flux boundary conditions in (1.3) are equivalent to the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions,

∇uaε⋅σ=∇ubε⋅σ=∇vε⋅σ=0,on (0,+∞)×∂Ω\nabla u_{a}^{\varepsilon}\cdot\sigma=\nabla u_{b}^{\varepsilon}\cdot\sigma=\nabla v^{\varepsilon}\cdot\sigma=0\hskip 2.84544pt,\hskip 9.24994pt\text{on }(0,+\infty)\times\,\partial\Omega\,

(see [20] for similar diffusion operator for a single species with two phenotypes). However, after taking the singular limit, we obtain the zero flux boundary conditions (1.9), but not the homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.

If da=dbd_{a}=d_{b}, the diffusion for the species uu given in (1.6) is the homogeneous linear diffusion. However, the diffusivity of a species usually depends on its food (or prey) and da≠dbd_{a}\neq d_{b} in general. In that case (da≠dbd_{a}\neq d_{b}), the diffusion for the total population in (1.6) contains cross-diffusion dynamics depending on the distribution of the three populations groups, ua,ubu_{a},u_{b} and vv, through the relations in (1.7). This explains the starvation-driven diffusion for the specific case of the paper, a concept formally introduced by Cho and Kim [7]. Funaki et al. [18] derived a macroscopic cross-diffusion model from a system of two phenotypes and a signaling chemical in the context of chemotaxis.

The proof of the convergence as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 is rigorously obtained via a priori estimates for uaε,ubε,u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon}, and vεv^{\varepsilon}. The main tool is the energy (or entropy) functional

ℰ⁡(ua,ub,v):=∫Ωh1​(ua)​𝑑x+∫Ωh2​(ub,v)​𝑑x,\mathcal{E}(u_{a},u_{b},v):=\int_{\Omega}h_{1}(u_{a})\,dx+\int_{\Omega}h_{2}(u_{b},v)\,dx\,, (1.10)

where

h1​(ua):=∫0uaψ⁡(za)​z​𝑑z,and​h2​(ub,v):=∫0ubϕ⁡(z+vb)​z​𝑑z.h_{1}(u_{a}):=\int_{0}^{u_{a}}\psi\Big(\dfrac{z}{a}\Big)\,z\,dz,\hskip 9.24994pt\text{and}\hskip 9.24994pth_{2}(u_{b},v):=\int_{0}^{u_{b}}\phi\Big(\dfrac{z+v}{b}\Big)z\,dz\,. (1.11)

Notice here that the assumption (H1) implies that h1h_{1} is positive, increasing, and convex, and that h2h_{2} is positive, increasing in both variables, and convex with respect to the first variable. Therefore, the name entropy for the function given in (1.10) is justified. We refer to [10] and [15] for the use of such entropies in the context of triangular cross-diffusion systems (that is, systems in which only one of the two equations includes a cross-diffusion term). For more general systems, we refer to [5, 6, 12, 14, 21, 2] among other works.

Then, by invoking the Aubin-Lions Lemma, we pass to the limit along a subsequence and conclude that the limit is a weak solution of (1.6)–(1.9). To use the energy estimate, we take initial values with bounded energy, which is our second hypothesis

  • (H2)

    uain∈L+1​(Ω)u_{a}^{\text{in}}\in L^{1}_{+}(\Omega), ubin∈L+1​(Ω)u_{b}^{\text{in}}\in L^{1}_{+}(\Omega), vin∈L+∞​(Ω)v^{\text{in}}\in L^{\infty}_{+}(\Omega), and ℰ⁡(uain,ubin,vin)<∞\mathcal{E}(u^{\text{in}}_{a},u^{\text{in}}_{b},v^{\text{in}})<\infty.

Remark 1.

Under Hypothesis (H2), the initial data uain,ubin,vinu_{a}^{\text{in}},u_{b}^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}} for the reaction diffusion system (1.1) do not satisfy a priori the nonlinear equation Q⁡(uain,ubin,vin)=0Q(u_{a}^{\text{in}},u_{b}^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}})=0 in (1.7). Thus, the appearance of an initial layer is expected (see also Section 5).

We conclude this introduction proposing a formal derivation of (1.1) out of a microscopic system. We shall consider problems left open here (such as regularity, uniqueness, stability and long time asymptotic behaviour of the macroscopic solutions) in a forthcoming paper, where a more general class of cross-diffusion system is analysed.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 is devoted to the statement of the existence result. In Section 3.1, we prove a priori estimates, which are the preliminary ingredients for the proof of the existence result obtained in Section 3.2. The paper concludes with the existence and linear stability analysis of trivial and non-trivial spatially homogeneous steady states, in Section 4 and Appendix A, with a particular emphasis put on the coexistence state. Some numerical tests in Section 5 illustrate the linear stability analysis. The discussion in Section 6 completes the article.

1.2 Formal derivation of the reaction-diffusion system with fast switching

We explain here how the mesoscopic scale model (1.1) is obtained at a formal level from a microscopic scale model in which the resources inducing the competition explicitly appear. Consider

{∂ts1=1δ​[r1​s1​(1−s1A1)−p1​s1​U1]∂ts2=1δ​[r2​s2​(1−s2A2)−p2​s2​U2−pV​s2​V]∂tU1=D1​Δ​U1+k1​p1​s1​U1+1ε​[Φ⁡(p2​U2+pV​Vs2)​U2−Ψ⁡(p1​U1s1)​U1]∂tU2=D2​Δ​U2+k2​p2​s2​U2−1ε​[Φ⁡(p2​U2+pV​Vs2)​U2−Ψ⁡(p1​U1s1)​U1]∂tV=DV​Δ​V+kV​pV​s2​V,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}s_{1}=\dfrac{1}{\delta}\Big[r_{1}s_{1}\Big(1-\dfrac{s_{1}}{A_{1}}\Big)-p_{1}s_{1}U_{1}\Big]\\[5.81247pt] \partial_{t}s_{2}=\dfrac{1}{\delta}\Big[r_{2}s_{2}\Big(1-\dfrac{s_{2}}{A_{2}}\Big)-p_{2}s_{2}U_{2}-p_{V}s_{2}V\Big]\\[5.81247pt] \partial_{t}U_{1}=D_{1}\Delta U_{1}+k_{1}p_{1}s_{1}U_{1}+\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\Big[\Phi\Big(\dfrac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{s_{2}}\Big)U_{2}-\Psi\Big(\dfrac{p_{1}U_{1}}{s_{1}}\Big)U_{1}\Big]\\[5.81247pt] \partial_{t}U_{2}=D_{2}\Delta U_{2}+k_{2}p_{2}s_{2}U_{2}-\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\Big[\Phi\Big(\dfrac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{s_{2}}\Big)U_{2}-\Psi\Big(\dfrac{p_{1}U_{1}}{s_{1}}\Big)U_{1}\Big]\\[5.81247pt] \partial_{t}V=D_{V}\Delta V+k_{V}p_{V}s_{2}V,\end{cases} (1.12)

where δ>0\delta>0 is the microscopic reaction time scale and ε\varepsilon is the mesoscopic one (hence δ≪ε≪1\delta\ll\varepsilon\ll 1). These equations describe the time evolution of a small ecosystem with two prey population densities (or vegetal resources), s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}, and two predator population densities (or harvesters of the vegetal resources), UU and VV. Moreover, the population UU is composed of two subpopulations U1U_{1} and U2U_{2} depending on the prey they consume, i.e., s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}, respectively. The prey species sis_{i} follows the logistic dynamics with a carrying capacity AiA_{i} and an intrinsic growth rate rir_{i}. The predator species consume a certain amount of preys which is proportional to the prey density with proportionality factors p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} and pVp_{V}. The harvested prey mass is converted to the predator mass with conversion rates k1,k2k_{1},k_{2} and kVk_{V}. The subpopulations U1U_{1} and U2U_{2} convert to each other depending on the availability of the prey. The two functions Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi are the conversion rates which are respectively increasing functions of the starvation measures p2​U2+pV​Vs2\frac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{s_{2}} and p1​U1s1\frac{p_{1}U_{1}}{s_{1}}. The other species VV consumes only the second prey s2s_{2}. Hence, the active competition is only between VV and U2U_{2}, while U1U_{1} competes with VV passively (via conversion). Finally, since the dispersal rate of a predator species usually depends on the nature of its prey, D1≠D2D_{1}\neq D_{2} in general.

Remark 2.

The expression (1.12) has no diffusion terms for the prey species s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}. Since growth is the dominant factor for plant species and their dispersal is negligible, this is especially relevant when the prey species are vegetal resources. Mathematically, this choice yields an explicit form in the singular limits δ→0\delta\to 0, see (1.13). Adding diffusion terms in the prey species equations could result in a less explicit formulas.

The mescoscopic system with fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 is obtained in the limit δ→0\delta\to 0. This is to say that the time-scale for the reaction of the resources s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} is much faster than all other processes. In simple predator-prey models this corresponds to a fast dynamics of the prey which has been studied more carefully in [30, 24, 28].

In this formal limit δ→0\delta\to 0, we find

s1​(r1−r1​s1A1−p1​U1)=0⟹s1=0​ or ​s1=A1​(1−p1​U1r1),s_{1}\Big(r_{1}-\frac{r_{1}s_{1}}{A_{1}}-p_{1}U_{1}\Big)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ s_{1}=0\ \mbox{ or }\ s_{1}=A_{1}\Big(1-\frac{p_{1}U_{1}}{r_{1}}\Big),

and

s2​[r2​(1−s2A2)−p2​U2−pV​V]=0⟹s2=0​ or ​s2=A2​(1−p2​U2+pV​Vr2).s_{2}\Big[r_{2}\big(1-\frac{s_{2}}{A_{2}}\big)-p_{2}U_{2}-p_{V}V\Big]=0\ \Longrightarrow\ s_{2}=0\ \mbox{ or }\ s_{2}=A_{2}\Big(1-\frac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{r_{2}}\Big).

Only the nontrivial case, s1≠0≠s2s_{1}\neq 0\neq s_{2}, is meaningful (since s1=0s_{1}=0 and s2=0s_{2}=0 correspond to unstable equilibria), and we obtain two relations

p1​U1s1=r1s1−r1A1​and​p2​U2+pV​Vs2=r2s2−r2A2.\frac{p_{1}U_{1}}{s_{1}}=\frac{r_{1}}{s_{1}}-\frac{r_{1}}{A_{1}}\hskip 9.24994pt\mbox{and}\hskip 9.24994pt\frac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{s_{2}}=\frac{r_{2}}{s_{2}}-\frac{r_{2}}{A_{2}}.

Therefore, the last three equations in (1.12) turn into

{∂tU1=D1​Δ​U1+A1​k1​p1​U1​(1−p1​U1r1)+1ε​[Φ​U2−Ψ​U1]∂tU2=D2​Δ​U2+A2​k2​p2​U2​(1−p2​U2+pV​Vr2)−1ε​[Φ​U2−Ψ​U1]∂tV=DV​Δ​V+A2​kV​pV​V​(1−p2​U2+pV​Vr2),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}U_{1}=D_{1}\Delta U_{1}+A_{1}k_{1}p_{1}U_{1}\big(1-\frac{p_{1}U_{1}}{r_{1}}\big)+\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\big[\Phi U_{2}-\Psi U_{1}\big]\\[7.74997pt] \partial_{t}U_{2}=D_{2}\Delta U_{2}+A_{2}k_{2}p_{2}U_{2}\,\big(1-\frac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{r_{2}}\big)-\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\big[\Phi U_{2}-\Psi U_{1}\big]\\[7.74997pt] \partial_{t}V\,=D_{V}\Delta V+A_{2}k_{V}p_{V}V\,\big(1-\frac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{r_{2}}\big),\end{cases} (1.13)

where the conversion rates Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi read as

Φ=Φ⁡(r2s2−r2A2)​and​Ψ=Ψ⁡(r1s1−r1A1),\Phi=\Phi\Big(\frac{r_{2}}{s_{2}}-\frac{r_{2}}{A_{2}}\Big)\hskip 9.24994pt\text{and}\hskip 9.24994pt\Psi=\Psi\Big(\frac{r_{1}}{s_{1}}-\frac{r_{1}}{A_{1}}\Big)\,,

and the Lotka-Volterra reaction dynamics of competition type naturally appears.

Now we consider the relationship between the variables in (1.1) and in (1.13). First, we define

uaε:=U1,ubε:=U2,vε:=pVp2​V,u_{a}^{\varepsilon}:=U_{1},\ u_{b}^{\varepsilon}:=U_{2},\ v^{\varepsilon}:=\frac{p_{V}}{p_{2}}V\,,

and keep the same diffusivity coefficients

da:=D1,db:=D2,dv:=DV.d_{a}:=D_{1},\ d_{b}:=D_{2},\ d_{v}:=D_{V}\,.

Then, the coefficients in the Lotka-Volterra type competition dynamics, fa,fbf_{a},f_{b} and fvf_{v}, are given as

ηa:=p1​A1​k1,ηb:=p2​A2​k2,ηv:=pV​A2​kV,a:=r1p1,b:=r2p2.\eta_{a}:=p_{1}A_{1}k_{1},\hskip 9.24994pt\eta_{b}:=p_{2}A_{2}k_{2},\hskip 9.24994pt\eta_{v}:=p_{V}A_{2}k_{V},\hskip 9.24994pta:=\dfrac{r_{1}}{p_{1}},\hskip 9.24994ptb:=\dfrac{r_{2}}{p_{2}}. (1.14)

Finally, the mesoscopic conversion rates are as follows

ϕ⁡(x):=Φ⁡(r2A2​x1−x),ψ⁡(x):=Ψ⁡(r1A1​x1−x).\phi(x):=\Phi\Big(\frac{r_{2}}{A_{2}}\frac{x}{1-x}\Big),\hskip 9.24994pt\psi(x):=\Psi\Big(\frac{r_{1}}{A_{1}}\frac{x}{1-x}\Big). (1.15)

After replacing variables, coefficients and functions with the above new ones, system (1.13) becomes our system (1.1).

Remark 3.

(i)(i) The conversion rates of the microscopic model, Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi, are functions of the starvation measures p2​U2+pV​Vs2\frac{p_{2}U_{2}+p_{V}V}{s_{2}} and p1​U1s1\frac{p_{1}U_{1}}{s_{1}}, instead of simply U2+Vs2\frac{U_{2}+V}{s_{2}} and U1s1\frac{U_{1}}{s_{1}}, in order to take into account the difference in the harvesting rates p2p_{2} and pVp_{V}. (i​i)(ii) The mesoscopic conversion rates ϕ\phi and ψ\psi in (1.15) are increasing functions, since Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi are chosen to be increasing functions. (i​i​i)(iii) It is worth noticing that the carrying capacities aa and bb for the predator species are proportional to the growth rates rir_{i}’s of the prey species and that the prey carrying capacities AiA_{i}’s are also involved in deciding ϕ\phi and ψ\psi (see (1.14) and (1.15)). (i​v)(iv) The macroscopic system reduces to the classical Lotka-Volterra system of competition type with linear diffusion, whenever the conversion rates ϕ\phi and ψ\psi are both constant, (see the discussion section 6).

2 Statement of the main result

Before stating our main result in Theorem 2.2 below, we introduce some notations that will be used in the sequel, and the definition of the very weak solutions of (1.6)–(1.9), with the reaction terms in (1.4).

We denote

We observe that all terms in (2.2)–(2.3) are well-defined thanks to the assumptions (H2) on the initial densities uin,vinu^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}}, to the L2L^{2} integrability of the sub-population densities ua,ubu_{a},u_{b} and to the L∞L^{\infty} bound for vv. Remember that the logistic structure of the reaction functions fa,fb,fvf_{a},f_{b},f_{v} involves at most quadratic nonlinearities.

Theorem 2.2.

Let Ω\Omega be a smooth bounded domain of ℝN\,\mathbb{R}^{\mathrm{N}}, N≥1\mathrm{N}\geq 1. Assume (H1) and (H2) on parameters and initial data uain,ubinu_{a}^{\text{in}},u_{b}^{\text{in}}, vinv^{\text{in}}, respectively. We denote (uaε,ubε,vε)(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) the unique global strong (for t>0t>0) solution of system (1.1)–(1.3) with those initial data. Then, the triplet (uaε,ubε,vε)(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) converges a.e. (t,x)∈(0,+∞)×Ω(t,x)\in(0,+\infty)\times\,\Omega (up to extraction of a subsequence) towards a nonnegative triplet (ua,ub,v)(u_{a},u_{b},v), as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Moreover, the functions u:=ua+ubu:=u_{a}+u_{b}, vv satisfy the nonlinear system (1.7), for a.e. (t,x)∈(0,+∞)×Ω(t,x)\in(0,+\infty)\times\Omega, and the following bounds: u∈Lq​(ΩT)u\in L^{q}(\Omega_{T}) for q=2+2/Nq=2+2/\mathrm{N} if N≥3\mathrm{N}\geq 3, q<3q<3 if N=2\mathrm{N}=2 and q=3q=3 if N=1\mathrm{N}=1; v∈L∞​(ΩT)v\in L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T}); |∇u|∈L2​(ΩT)|\nabla u|\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}); and for the same previous qq, |∇v|∈L2​q​(ΩT)|\nabla v|\in L^{2q}(\Omega_{T}); ∂xi,xjv,∂tv∈Lq​(ΩT)\partial_{x_{i},x_{j}}v\,,\partial_{t}v\in L^{q}(\Omega_{T}), i,j=1,…,Ni,j=1,\dots,\mathrm{N}. Finally, (u,v)(u,v) is a very weak solution of the macroscopic system (1.6)–(1.9) with the reaction terms (1.4), in the sense of Definition 2.1.

3 Proof of the main Theorem

We first recall that for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a unique global strong (for t>0t>0) solution (uaε,ubε,vε)(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) solution to system (1.1)–(1.3), under the assumption on the initial data of Theorem 2.2. We refer for example to [13, 29] for obtaining such a result.

3.1 A priori estimates

In this section we shall obtain a priori estimates on the subpopulation densities uaε,ubεu_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon}, on the total population densities uε≔uaε+ubεu^{\varepsilon}\coloneqq u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon} and vεv^{\varepsilon}, and on Q⁡(uaε,ubε,vε)Q(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}). More specifically, we take advantage of the triangular structure of the system that give us a priori estimates on the density vεv^{\varepsilon} and its derivatives (see Lemma 3.1). The reaction functions faf_{a} and fbf_{b} of competition type allow us to control the total mass ∫Ωuε​(t)​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}u^{\varepsilon}(t)\,dx, and to get an L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) estimate on uεu^{\varepsilon} (see Lemma 3.2). The latter will be employed in Lemma 3.3 to obtain estimates on ∇uaε\nabla u_{a}^{\varepsilon}, ∇ubε\nabla u_{b}^{\varepsilon} and Q⁡(uaε,ubε,vε)Q(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}), through the use of the energy functional (1.10)–(1.11). In addition, the triplet (uaε,ubε,vε)(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) will be shown to have finite energy ℰ⁡(T)\mathcal{E}(T) as well, for all T>0T>0.

Hereafter, all constants CC and CTC_{T} are strictly positive and may depend on Ω\Omega, the initial data uain,ubin,vinu_{a}^{\text{in}},u_{b}^{\text{in}},v^{\text{in}}, the coefficients in system (1.1), the transition functions ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi and on TT, but never on ε\varepsilon. They may change also from line to line in the computations.

It is easily seen that

so that estimate (3.2) holds. Then, thanks to the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality [27], for all q∈(1,+∞)q\in(1,+\infty), there exists C⁡(q)>0C(q)>0, such that, for all t>0t>0 and i=1,…​Ni=1,\dots\mathrm{N}, we have

Corollary 3.4.

Under the hypothesis of Theorem 2.2, for all T>0T>0, the following estimates hold:

q:={2+2/Nif ​N>2,3,if ​N=1.q:=\begin{cases}2+2/\mathrm{N}&\mbox{if }\,\mathrm{N}>2,\\ 3,\hskip 42.67912pt&\mbox{if }\,\mathrm{N}=1.\end{cases} (3.21)

and q<3q<3 if N=2\mathrm{N}=2.

Proof.

The following argument is performed for the subpopulation uaεu^{\varepsilon}_{a}. It can be applied similarly to ubεu^{\varepsilon}_{b} and thus to uaε+ubεu^{\varepsilon}_{a}+u^{\varepsilon}_{b}.

Lemma 3.2 and 3.3 give that uaεu_{a}^{\varepsilon} is bounded in L2​([0,T],H1​(Ω))L^{2}([0,T];\,H^{1}(\Omega)). Thus, by the Sobolev embedding theorem, we have that uaεu_{a}^{\varepsilon} is bounded in L2​([0,T],LN∗​(Ω))L^{2}([0,T];\,L^{\mathrm{N}^{*}}(\Omega)), with N∗=2​NN−2\mathrm{N}^{*}=\frac{2\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{N}-2} if N>2\mathrm{N}>2, N∗∈[2,+∞)\mathrm{N}^{*}\in[2,+\infty) if N=2\mathrm{N}=2 and N∗=∞\mathrm{N}^{*}=\infty if N=1\mathrm{N}=1. Since we also know that uaεu_{a}^{\varepsilon} is bounded in L∞​([0,T],L1​(Ω))L^{\infty}([0,T];\,L^{1}(\Omega)), by interpolation we obtain that uaεu_{a}^{\varepsilon} is bounded in Lq​(ΩT)L^{q}(\Omega_{T}), with qq as in (3.21). ∎

At this point, using Lemma 3.1 again, we see that ∂tvε\partial_{t}v^{\varepsilon} and ∇∇vε\nabla\nabla v^{\varepsilon} are bounded in Lq​(ΩT)L^{q}(\Omega_{T}).

3.2 End of the proof of the main result

End of the proof of Theorem 2.2.

The proof is divided in four steps and uses compactness to identify limits along subsequences. The first and the second one focus on the identification of the limit (as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0) of the densities vεv^{\varepsilon} and uε=uaε+ubεu^{\varepsilon}=u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon}, a.e. in [0,T]×Ω[0,T]\times\Omega, respectively. In the third step we obtain the a.e. convergence of the subpopulation densities uaε,ubεu^{\varepsilon}_{a},u^{\varepsilon}_{b} and we identify the obtained limit as the unique solution of the nonlinear system (1.7). The convergence argument is also extended globally in time by a diagonal argument. Finally, the proof is concluded in the fourth step, taking the limit as ε\varepsilon tends to zero, in the very weak formulation of the system satisfied by uε=uaε+ubεu^{\varepsilon}=u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon} and vεv^{\varepsilon}.

First step. Let T>0T>0 be arbitrarily fixed. Thanks to the control of the density vεv^{\varepsilon} given in Lemma 3.1 and to the boundedness of uaε+ubεu_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon} in L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) obtained in Lemma 3.2, we have that (vε)ε(v^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} is bounded in L4​([0,T],W1,4​(Ω))L^{4}([0,T];W^{1,4}(\Omega)) and (∂tvε)ε(\partial_{t}v^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} is bounded in L2​([0,T],L2​(Ω))L^{2}([0,T];L^{2}(\Omega)). Therefore, by applying Rellich’s Theorem, there exists a subsequence, still denoted vεv^{\varepsilon}, and v∈L4​(ΩT)v\in L^{4}(\Omega_{T}) such that, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0,

vε​(t,x)⟶v⁡(t,x),a.e. on ​[0,T]×Ω.v^{\varepsilon}(t,x)\longrightarrow v(t,x)\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{a.e. on }[0,T]\times\Omega\,. (3.22)

Moreover,

∇vε⇀∇vin ​L4​(ΩT),\nabla v^{\varepsilon}\rightharpoonup\nabla v\,\,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{in }L^{4}(\Omega_{T}), (3.23)

and due to Lemma 3.1 again, vv is nonnegative and belongs to L∞​(ΩT),L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T}), while ∇v\nabla v lies in L4​(ΩT)L^{4}(\Omega_{T}).

Second step. We rewrite the parabolic equation satisfied by the density uε=uaε+ubεu^{\varepsilon}=u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon} as

∂tuε=Δ⁡(da​uaε+db​ubε)+fa​(uaε)+fb​(ubε,vε).\partial_{t}u^{\varepsilon}=\Delta(d_{a}\,u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+d_{b}\,u_{b}^{\varepsilon})+f_{a}(u_{a}^{\varepsilon})+f_{b}(u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon})\,. (3.24)

Thanks to Corollary 3.4, we see that (uε)ε(u^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon} is uniformly bounded in L2​([0,T],H1​(Ω))L^{2}([0,T];H^{1}(\Omega)) and in L2+2​δ​(ΩT)L^{2+2\delta}(\Omega_{T}) for some δ>0\delta>0, so that the reaction term in (3.24) is uniformly bounded in L1+δ​(ΩT)L^{1+\delta}(\Omega_{T}). Then (∂t(uaε+ubε))ε(\partial_{t}(u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon}))_{\varepsilon} is uniformly bounded in

L1+δ​([0,T],W−1,1+δ​(Ω))L^{1+\delta}([0,T];W^{-1,1+\delta}(\Omega)). Thus, Aubin-Lions’ lemma (cf. [26]) yields a subsequence (still denoted uεu^{\varepsilon}), and a function u≥0,u∈L2​(ΩT)u\geq 0,\,u\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}), such that, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0,

uε​(t,x)=uaε​(t,x)+ubε​(t,x)⟶u⁡(t,x),a. e. in ​ΩT,u^{\varepsilon}(t,x)=u_{a}^{\varepsilon}(t,x)+u_{b}^{\varepsilon}(t,x)\longrightarrow u(t,x)\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{a. e. in }\Omega_{T}\,, (3.25)

where the nonnegativity of uu follows from that of uεu^{\varepsilon}. Furthermore,

∇uε⇀∇uin ​L2​(ΩT),\nabla u^{\varepsilon}\,\rightharpoonup\,\nabla u\,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T})\,, (3.26)

and

∥u∥L2(ΩT)\displaystyle\Arrowvert u\,\Arrowvert_{L^{{}^{2}}(\Omega_{T})} =limε→ 0∥uaε+ubε∥L2(ΩT)⩽CT,\displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow\,0}\,\Arrowvert\,u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon}\,\Arrowvert_{L^{{}^{2}}(\Omega_{T})}\leqslant C_{T}\,,
∥∇u∥L2(ΩT)\displaystyle\Arrowvert\nabla u\,\Arrowvert_{L^{{}^{2}}(\Omega_{T})} ≤lim infε→ 0∥∇uε∥L2(ΩT)⩽CT.\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{\varepsilon\rightarrow\,0}\,\Arrowvert\,\nabla u^{\varepsilon}\,\Arrowvert_{L^{{}^{2}}(\Omega_{T})}\leqslant C_{T}\,.

Third step. The energy estimate (3.10) yields the estimate

∥ϕ(ubε+vεb)ubε−ψ(uaεa)uaε∥L2​(ΩT)≤εCT.\Big\Arrowvert\phi\Big(\dfrac{u^{\varepsilon}_{b}+v^{\varepsilon}}{b}\Big)u_{b}^{\varepsilon}-\psi\Big(\dfrac{u^{\varepsilon}_{a}}{a}\Big)u_{a}^{\varepsilon}\Big\Arrowvert_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,C_{T}\,. (3.27)

Let us denote (ua∗​(u,v),ub∗​(u,v))\big(u_{a}^{*}(u,v),u_{b}^{*}(u,v)\big) the unique solution of (1.7). Then, using the function qq defined in (2.1), we get

Finally, the proved convergence (3.25) and (3.22) and the continuity of ub∗u_{b}^{*} with respect to its arguments, yields the desired result, i.e.,

ubε→ub∗(u,v),uaε=uε−ubε→ua∗(u,v),ε→0, a.e. in ΩT.u_{b}^{\varepsilon}\to u_{b}^{*}(u,v)\,,\hskip 9.24994ptu_{a}^{\varepsilon}=u^{\varepsilon}-u_{b}^{\varepsilon}\to u_{a}^{*}(u,v)\,,\hskip 9.24994pt\varepsilon\to 0\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{ a.e. in }\,\,\Omega_{\,T}\,.

To conclude, let us remark that all the a.e. convergence results obtained so far have been performed on [0,T][0,T], for any arbitrary T>0T>0. Since (uaε,ubε,vε)(u_{a}^{\varepsilon},u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon}) is defined on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty), by extracting subsequences, these arguments can be replicated in the time intervals [0,2​T][0,2T], [0,3​T][0,3T], and so on. Then by Cantor’s diagonal argument, the convergences (3.22), (3.25) and (3.28), and the convergence of the pair (uaε,ubε)(u^{\varepsilon}_{a},u^{\varepsilon}_{b}) towards the solution of (1.7) are verified a.e. in (0,+∞)×Ω(0,+\infty)\times\Omega.

Fourth step. We shall prove now that (u,v)(u,v) is a weak solution of (1.6), in the sense of Definition 2.1. For this purpose, let us consider two test functions ξ1,ξ2\xi_{1},\xi_{2} in Cc2C_{c}^{2}, satisfying ∇ξ1⋅σ=∇ξ2⋅σ=0\nabla\xi_{1}\cdot\sigma=\nabla\xi_{2}\cdot\sigma=0, on [0,T]×∂Ω[0,T]\times\partial\Omega. Multiplying the equation satisfied by uaε+ubεu_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon} by ξ1\xi_{1} and the third equation of (1.1) by ξ2\xi_{2} and integrating over (0,+∞)×Ω(0,+\infty)\times\Omega, we get,

−∫0∞∫Ω(∂tξ1)(uaε+ubε)dxdt−∫Ωξ1(0)(uain,ε+ubin,ε)dx=∫0∞∫ΩΔ​ξ1​(da​uaε+db​ubε)​dx​dt+∫0∞∫Ωξ1​(fa​(uaε)+fb​(ubε,vε))​dx​dt,\begin{split}&-\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\,(\partial_{t}\xi_{1})\,(u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\varepsilon})\,dx\,dt-\int_{\Omega}\xi_{1}(0)\,\big(u_{a}^{\text{in},\varepsilon}+u_{b}^{\text{in},\varepsilon}\big)\,dx=\\ &\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\,\Delta\xi_{1}\,\big(\,d_{a}u_{a}^{\varepsilon}+d_{b}u_{b}^{\varepsilon}\,\big)\,dx\,dt+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\,\xi_{1}\big(f_{a}(u_{a}^{\varepsilon})+f_{b}(u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon})\big)\,dx\,dt\,,\end{split} (3.29)

and

−∫0∞∫Ω(∂tξ2)vεdxdt−∫Ωξ2​(0)​vin,ε​dx=dv​∫0∞∫ΩΔ​ξ2​vε​dx​dt+∫0∞∫Ωξ2​fv​(ubε,vε)​dx​dt.\begin{split}-\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\,(\partial_{t}\xi_{2}\,)\,v^{\varepsilon}\,dx&\,dt-\int_{\Omega}\xi_{2}(0)\,{v}^{\text{in},\varepsilon}\,dx=\\ &d_{v}\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\,\Delta\xi_{2}\,v^{\varepsilon}\,dx\,dt+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\,\xi_{2}\,f_{v}(u_{b}^{\varepsilon},v^{\varepsilon})\,dx\,dt\,.\end{split} (3.30)

Concerning the equation (3.29), the convergence results obtained in the previous steps and the estimates in (3.6) allow us to pass to the limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, in all the terms of the equation, using Lebesgue’s dominated convergence theorem, thus obtaining (2.2).

The same conclusion holds for equation (3.30). The proof of Theorem 2.2 is now completed. ∎

4 Linear stability analysis

In this section, we investigate the linear stability of spatially homogeneous steady states of the macroscopic system (1.6)–(1.9), with reaction and fast reaction functions given by (1.4) and (1.5), respectively. We shall also see the relationship between the linear stability of the coexistence steady state at the mesoscopic and macroscopic scale, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Let ψ\psi and ϕ\phi be conversion rates satisfying assumption (H1). We introduce the following few notations for later use,

ψ1=ψ⁡(1),ϕ1=ϕ⁡(1),\psi_{1}=\psi(1),\hskip 18.49988pt\phi_{1}=\phi(1)\,,

and the parameter providing a criterion for the linear stability (see Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.2),

α≔ψ1ϕ1​ab>0.\alpha\coloneqq\frac{\psi_{1}}{\phi_{1}}\,\frac{a}{b}>0\,. (4.1)

The pair (u¯,v¯)∈ℝ+2(\bar{u},\bar{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+} is a spatially homogeneous steady state of the macroscopic system if and only if u¯=u¯a+u¯b\bar{u}=\bar{u}_{a}+\bar{u}_{b} and the triplet (u¯a,u¯b,v¯)(\bar{u}_{a},\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v}) satisfy the nonlinear system

fa​(u¯a)+fb​(u¯b,v¯)=fv​(u¯b,v¯)=Q⁡(u¯a,u¯b,v¯)=0.f_{a}(\bar{u}_{a})+f_{b}(\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v})=f_{v}(\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v})=Q(\bar{u}_{a},\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v})=0\,. (4.2)

Extinction of uu. From Q⁡(u¯a,u¯b,v¯)=0Q(\bar{u}_{a},\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v})=0 and the strict positivity of ϕ\phi and ψ\psi, we see that u¯a=0\bar{u}_{a}=0 if and only if u¯b=0\bar{u}_{b}=0: no extinction of a single subpopulation of the species uu is admitted. Thus, for u¯a=u¯b=0\bar{u}_{a}=\bar{u}_{b}=0, we obtain the trivial and semi-trivial steady states

(u¯1,v¯1)=(0,0)and(u¯2,v¯2)=(0,b),(\bar{u}_{1},\bar{v}_{1})=(0,0)\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988pt(\bar{u}_{2},\bar{v}_{2})=(0,b)\,, (4.3)

corresponding to the total extinction of the two species in the ecosystem and to a partial extinction, respectively.

Survival of uu and extinction of vv. The other steady states with u¯a≠0\bar{u}_{a}\neq 0 and u¯b≠0\bar{u}_{b}\neq 0 are of main interest. The first case is with v¯=0\bar{v}=0. Denoting u¯a=λ​a\bar{u}_{a}=\lambda\,a and u¯b=σ​b\bar{u}_{b}=\sigma\,b, for λ,σ>0\lambda,\sigma>0, system (4.2) reduces to

ηa​a​λ​(1−λ)+ηb​b​σ​(1−σ)=0,λ​ψ​(λ)σ​ϕ​(σ)=ba.\eta_{a}a\,\lambda(1-\lambda)+\eta_{b}b\,\sigma(1-\sigma)=0\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\lambda\psi(\lambda)}{\sigma\phi(\sigma)}=\frac{b}{a}\,. (4.4)

Such a semi-trivial state always exists but the uniqueness is non-trivial. Indeed, the second equation in (4.4) can be written equivalently as

σ​ϕ​(σ)ϕ1=α​λ​ψ​(λ)ψ1.\frac{\sigma\phi(\sigma)}{\phi_{1}}=\alpha\,\frac{\lambda\psi(\lambda)}{\psi_{1}}\,. (4.5)

Due to assumption (H1), the functions Λ⁡(λ):=λ​ψ​(λ)/ψ1\Lambda(\lambda):=\lambda\psi(\lambda)/\psi_{1} and Σ⁡(σ):=σ​ϕ​(σ)/ϕ1\Sigma(\sigma):=\sigma\phi(\sigma)/\phi_{1} are strictly increasing functions from 0 to +∞+\infty. Hence, for every λ>0\lambda>0 there exists a unique σ⁡(λ)>0\sigma(\lambda)>0 solving (4.5) and given by

σ⁡(λ)=Σ−1​(α​Λ​(λ)).\sigma(\lambda)=\Sigma^{-1}(\alpha\Lambda(\lambda))\,. (4.6)

Plugging (4.6) into the left hand side equation in (4.4), the stationary states correspond to the zeros of the function FF below

F⁡(λ):=ηa​a​λ​(1−λ)+ηb​b​σ​(λ)​(1−σ⁡(λ)).F(\lambda):=\eta_{a}a\,\lambda(1-\lambda)+\eta_{b}b\,\sigma(\lambda)(1-\sigma(\lambda))\,. (4.7)

Furthermore, by the competition structure, it follows that FF is positive for small enough λ\lambda and F⁡(λ)→−∞F(\lambda)\to-\infty as λ→+∞\lambda\to+\infty. Thus, the macroscopic system (1.4)–(1.7) admits at least one semi-trivial equilibrium

(u¯3,v¯3)=(a​λ+b​σ,0),(\bar{u}_{3},\bar{v}_{3})=(a\lambda+b\sigma,0)\,, (4.8)

solution of system (4.4), with σ=σ⁡(λ)\sigma=\sigma(\lambda) uniquely determined by (4.6). Moreover, if the equilibrium is unique, FF is decreasing around the corresponding λ\lambda, i.e. F′​(λ)< 0F^{\prime}(\lambda)<\penalty\ 0.

In general it is possible to have several semi-trivial states of type (4.8). As an example, take

a=b=1,ηa=0.2,ηb=1,ϕ≡1,ψ⁡(x)={0.1if ​x≤1.6,0.3otherwise.a=b=1,\hskip 9.24994pt\eta_{a}=0.2,\hskip 9.24994pt\eta_{b}=1,\hskip 9.24994pt\phi\equiv 1,\hskip 9.24994pt\psi(x)=\begin{cases}0.1&\text{if }x\leq 1.6,\\ 0.3&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (4.9)

The corresponding F⁡(λ)F(\lambda) is shown in Figure 1, from where we see that there exist three semi-trivial states.

We will discuss the uniqueness issue in Proposition 4.2, where a sufficient condition for uniqueness of (4.8) is given, and Proposition 4.3, where we exhibit a family of conversion rates functions ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi for which uniqueness of (4.8) holds true.

Coexistence of uu and vv. Finally, if u¯a≠0\bar{u}_{a}\neq 0, u¯b≠0\bar{u}_{b}\neq 0, v¯≠0\bar{v}\neq 0, from fv​(u¯b,v¯)=0f_{v}(\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v})=0 we get u¯b+v¯=b\bar{u}_{b}+\bar{v}=b and thus u¯a=a\bar{u}_{a}=a. Then, from Q⁡(u¯a,u¯b,v¯)=0Q(\bar{u}_{a},\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v})=0 and the definition of α\alpha it follows that u¯b=b​α\bar{u}_{b}=b\alpha. Therefore, system (4.2) has a unique totally nontrivial solution given by

(u¯4,v¯4)=(a+b​α,b⁡(1−α)),(\bar{u}_{4},\bar{v}_{4})=(a+b\alpha,b(1-\alpha))\,, (4.10)

provided that α<1\alpha<1.

We shall see in the following subsection (see Theorem 4.1) that the stationary states (4.3) are unstable, so that the total extinction of the species uu never occurs. The species uu always survives and its coexistence with the species vv is conditioned by the switching strategy that the subpopulations uau_{a} and ubu_{b} adopt when both resources run out, quantified through the parameter α\alpha. Indeed, the coexistence occurs if the switch from the state ubu_{b} to the state uau_{a} is faster than the opposite switch, i.e. α<1\alpha<1. On the other hand, vv goes extinct only if α>1\alpha>1.

The relationship between the linear stability of the mesoscopic and macroscopic coexistence steady states, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, is seen in Subsection 4.3.

4.1 Linear stability analysis for the cross-diffusion system

Let us consider the partial starvation measures

λ=u¯aa≥0,σ=u¯bb≥0,δ=v¯b∈{0,1−σ},\lambda=\frac{\bar{u}_{a}}{a}\geq 0\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\sigma=\frac{\bar{u}_{b}}{b}\geq 0\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\delta=\frac{\bar{v}}{b}\in\{0,1-\sigma\}\,,\hskip 18.49988pt

so that each of the above steady states can be identified with the triplet (λ,σ,δ)(\lambda,\sigma,\delta) and written as

P¯=(u¯,v¯)=(λ​a+σ​b,δ​b).\bar{P}=(\bar{u},\bar{v})=\big(\lambda a+\sigma b,\delta b\big)\,. (4.11)

Linearizing around P¯\bar{P} the ODEs system associated to (1.4)–(1.7), in the sense of small perturbation τ\tau, |τ|≪1|\tau|\ll 1, i.e.

ua=u¯a+τ​u~a​and​ub=u¯b+τ​u~bu=ua+ub=(u¯a+u¯b)+τ⁡(u~a+u~b)=u¯+τ​u~,v=v¯+τ​v~,\begin{split}&u_{a}=\bar{u}_{a}+\tau\,\tilde{u}_{a}\hskip 9.24994pt\text{and}\hskip 9.24994ptu_{b}=\bar{u}_{b}+\tau\,\tilde{u}_{b}\\ &u=u_{a}+u_{b}=(\bar{u}_{a}+\bar{u}_{b})+\tau(\tilde{u}_{a}+\tilde{u}_{b})=\bar{u}+\tau\,\tilde{u},\\ &v=\bar{v}+\tau\tilde{v},\end{split} (4.12)

we obtain

{u~˙=ηa​(1−2​λ)​u~a+ηb​(1−2​σ−δ)​u~b−ηb​σ​v~+o⁡(1),v~˙=−ηv​δ​u~b+ηv​(1−σ−2​δ)​v~+o⁡(1).\begin{cases}\dot{\tilde{u}}=\eta_{a}(1-2\lambda)\tilde{u}_{a}+\eta_{b}(1-2\sigma-\delta)\tilde{u}_{b}-\eta_{b}\sigma\,\tilde{v}+o(1),\\ \dot{\tilde{v}}=-\eta_{v}\delta\,\tilde{u}_{b}+\eta_{v}(1-\sigma-2\delta)\tilde{v}+o(1).\end{cases} (4.13)

Moreover, from the linearization of Q⁡(ua,ub,v)Q(u_{a},u_{b},v) around (u¯a,u¯b,v¯),(\bar{u}_{a},\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v}), we have

∂1Q¯​u~a+∂2Q¯​u~b+∂3Q¯​v~+o⁡(1)=0,\partial_{1}\bar{Q}\,\tilde{u}_{a}+\partial_{2}\bar{Q}\,\tilde{u}_{b}+\partial_{3}\bar{Q}\,\tilde{v}+o(1)=0, (4.14)

where ∂jQ¯=∂jQ⁡(u¯a,u¯b,v¯)\partial_{j}\bar{Q}=\partial_{j}Q(\bar{u}_{a},\bar{u}_{b},\bar{v}) and

∂1Q¯=−ψ⁡(λ)−λ​ψ′​(λ)=:−β⁡(λ)<0,∂2Q¯=ϕ⁡(σ+δ)+σ​ϕ′​(σ+δ)=:γ⁡(σ,δ)>0,∂3Q¯=σ​ϕ′​(σ+δ)=:θ⁡(σ,δ)>0.\begin{split}\partial_{1}\bar{Q}&=-\psi(\lambda)-\lambda\psi^{\prime}(\lambda)=:-\beta(\lambda)<0\,,\\ \partial_{2}\bar{Q}&=\phi(\sigma+\delta)+\sigma\phi^{\prime}(\sigma+\delta)=:\gamma(\sigma,\delta)>0\,,\\ \partial_{3}\bar{Q}&=\sigma\phi^{\prime}(\sigma+\delta)=:\theta(\sigma,\delta)>0\,.\end{split} (4.15)

Using u~=u~a+u~b\tilde{u}=\tilde{u}_{a}+\tilde{u}_{b}, from (4.14) we obtain u~a\tilde{u}_{a} and u~b\tilde{u}_{b} in terms of u~\tilde{u} and v~\tilde{v} as follows

u~a=1r​γ​(σ,δ)​u~+1r​θ​(σ,δ)​v~+o⁡(1),u~b=1r​β​(λ)​u~−1r​θ​(σ,δ)​v~+o⁡(1),\tilde{u}_{a}=\frac{1}{r}\,\gamma(\sigma,\delta)\,\tilde{u}+\frac{1}{r}\,\theta(\sigma,\delta)\,\tilde{v}+o(1)\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\tilde{u}_{b}=\frac{1}{r}\,\beta(\lambda)\,\tilde{u}-\frac{1}{r}\,\theta(\sigma,\delta)\,\tilde{v}+o(1)\,, (4.16)

where r=r⁡(λ,σ,δ)≔∂2Q¯−∂1Q¯=β⁡(λ)+γ⁡(σ,δ)>0r=r(\lambda,\sigma,\delta)\coloneqq\partial_{2}\bar{Q}-\partial_{1}\bar{Q}=\beta(\lambda)+\gamma(\sigma,\delta)>0. Thus, system (4.13) becomes

w~˙=M¯​w~+o⁡(1),w~≔(u~v~),\dot{\tilde{w}}=\bar{M}\,\tilde{w}+o(1),\hskip 18.49988pt\hskip 18.49988pt\tilde{w}\coloneqq\begin{pmatrix}\,\tilde{u}\,\\ \,\tilde{v}\,\end{pmatrix},

and the matrix M¯=M⁡(P¯)\bar{M}=M(\bar{P}) has the following entries

M11​(P¯)=ηar​(1−2​λ)​γ​(σ,δ)+ηbr​(1−2​σ−δ)​β​(λ),M12​(P¯)=ηar​(1−2​λ)​θ​(σ,δ)−ηbr​(1−2​σ−δ)​θ​(σ,δ)−ηb​σ,M21​(P¯)=−ηvr​δ​β​(λ),M22​(P¯)=ηvr​δ​θ​(σ,δ)+ηv​(1−σ−2​δ).\begin{split}M_{11}(\bar{P})&=\frac{\eta_{a}}{r}(1-2\lambda)\gamma(\sigma,\delta)+\frac{\eta_{b}}{r}(1-2\sigma-\delta)\beta(\lambda)\,,\\ M_{12}(\bar{P})&=\frac{\eta_{a}}{r}(1-2\lambda)\theta(\sigma,\delta)-\frac{\eta_{b}}{r}(1-2\sigma-\delta)\theta(\sigma,\delta)-\eta_{b}\sigma\,,\\ M_{21}(\bar{P})&=-\frac{\eta_{v}}{r}\delta\,\beta(\lambda)\,,\\ M_{22}(\bar{P})&=\frac{\eta_{v}}{r}\delta\,\theta(\sigma,\delta)+\eta_{v}(1-\sigma-2\delta)\,.\end{split} (4.17)

Next, for uau_{a} and ubu_{b} as in (4.12), using (4.16) again, the linearization of the cross-diffusion operator in (1.6) reads as

Δ⁡(da​ua+db​ub)=τ⁡(da​γ⁡(σ,δ)r+db​β⁡(λ)r)​Δ​u~+τ⁡(da−db)​θ⁡(σ,δ)r​Δ​v~+o⁡(τ),\Delta\big(d_{a}u_{a}+d_{b}u_{b}\big)=\tau\Big(d_{a}\frac{\gamma(\sigma,\delta)}{r}+d_{b}\frac{\beta(\lambda)}{r}\Big)\Delta\tilde{u}+\tau(d_{a}-d_{b})\frac{\theta(\sigma,\delta)}{r}\Delta\tilde{v}+o(\tau),

and the linearized cross-diffusion macroscopic system writes

with

The homogeneous (up to a o⁡(1)o(1) term) Neumann boundary conditions for w~\tilde{w} in (4.18) follow by the no flux boundary condition (1.9) and (4.16).

Neglecting the o⁡(1)o(1) terms, the stability of the linearized system (4.18) can be analysed decomposing w~​(t,x)\tilde{w}(t,x) as

w~​(t,x)=∑n∈ℕw~n​(t)​en​(x),\tilde{w}(t,x)=\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\tilde{w}_{n}(t)\,e_{n}(x)\,,

where (en)n∈ℕ(e_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is the orthogonal eigenbasis of −Δ-\Delta on Ω\Omega with Neumann boundary conditions. Denoting 0=λ0<λ1≤⋯≤λn≤⋯0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\dots\leq\lambda_{n}\leq\dotsb the corresponding eigenvalues, the projection coefficients w~n​(t)\tilde{w}_{n}(t) evolve independently according the equations

∂tw~n​(t)=(−λn​J¯+M¯)​w~n​(t),n∈ℕ.\partial_{t}\tilde{w}_{n}(t)=(-\lambda_{n}\bar{J}+\bar{M})\tilde{w}_{n}(t)\,,\hskip 18.49988ptn\in{\mathbb{N}}\,.

Thus, for the stability analysis it suffices to consider the stability of the matrix Nn≔−λn​J¯+M¯N_{n}\coloneqq-\lambda_{n}\bar{J}+\bar{M}, i.e.

Nn=[−1r​(da​γ+db​β)​λn+M11−1r​(da−db)​θ​λn+M12M21−dv​λn+M22],N_{n}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{r}\big(d_{a}\,\gamma+d_{b}\beta\big)\lambda_{n}+M_{11}\hskip 9.24994pt&\hskip 9.24994pt-\frac{1}{r}(d_{a}-d_{b})\theta\,\lambda_{n}+M_{12}\\[5.81247pt] M_{21}&-d_{v}\lambda_{n}+M_{22}\end{bmatrix}, (4.19)

with Mi​j=Mi​j​(P¯)M_{ij}=M_{ij}(\bar{P}) defined in (4.17).

Theorem 4.1.

Let ψ\psi and ϕ\phi be conversion rates satisfying assumption (H1) and α>0\alpha>0 defined as in (4.1). Then, the following holds true.

  • (i)

    The trivial and semi-trivial steady states (u¯1,v¯1)=(0,0)(\bar{u}_{1},\bar{v}_{1})=(0,0) and (u¯2,v¯2)=(0,b)(\bar{u}_{2},\bar{v}_{2})=(0,b) are linearly unstable.

  • (ii)

    The family of semi-trivial steady states (u¯3,v¯3)=(a​λ+b​σ,0)(\bar{u}_{3},\bar{v}_{3})=(a\lambda+b\sigma,0) satisfies

    σ=λ=1,if ​α=1,\sigma=\lambda=1\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{if }\alpha=1\,, (4.20)
    0<σ<1<λ<12+12​1+b​ηba​ηa,if ​α<1,0<\sigma<1<\lambda<\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+\frac{b\eta_{b}}{a\eta_{a}}}\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{if }\alpha<1\,, (4.21)

    and the swapped relation

    0<λ<1<σ<12+12​1+a​ηab​ηb,if ​α>1.0<\lambda<1<\sigma<\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+\frac{a\eta_{a}}{b\eta_{b}}}\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{if }\alpha>1\,. (4.22)

    Furthermore, they are linearly unstable if α≤1\alpha\leq 1, and if α>1\alpha>1, they are linearly stable if and only if the function FF in (4.7) is strictly decreasing around λ\lambda, i.e. F′​(λ)<0F^{\prime}(\lambda)<0.

  • (iii)

    If α<1\alpha<1, there exists a unique strictly positive steady state given by (u¯4,v¯4)=(a+b​α,b⁡(1−α))(\bar{u}_{4},\bar{v}_{4})=(a+b\alpha,b(1-\alpha)) and it is linearly stable.

Proof.

(i) From (4.17) and (4.15), we have

M⁡(0,0)=diag​{ηa​ϕ​(0)+ηb​ψ​(0)ϕ⁡(0)+ψ⁡(0),ηv}andM⁡(0,b)=[ηa​ϕ1ϕ1+ψ⁡(0) 0−ηv​ψ​(0)ϕ1+ψ⁡(0)−ηv],M(0,0)=\text{diag}\Big\{\frac{\eta_{a}\phi(0)+\eta_{b}\psi(0)}{\phi(0)+\psi(0)},\,\eta_{v}\Big\}\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988ptM(0,b)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\eta_{a}\phi_{1}}{\phi_{1}+\psi(0)}\,&\,0\\ -\frac{\eta_{v}\psi(0)}{\phi_{1}+\psi(0)}\,&\,-\eta_{v}\end{bmatrix},

implying that the steady states (0,0)(0,0) and (0,b)(0,b) are linearly unstable, both for the macroscopic system and for the associated diffusion-less one, because of the zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian.

(ii) In order to proceed with the investigation of the family of steady states (u¯3,v¯3)=(a​λ+b​σ,0)(\bar{u}_{3},\bar{v}_{3})=(a\lambda+b\sigma,0), let us observe that from the first equation in (4.4), we have

(1−λ)​(1−σ)<0​or​λ=σ=1.(1-\lambda)(1-\sigma)<0\hskip 9.24994pt\text{or}\hskip 9.24994pt\lambda=\sigma=1\,. (4.23)

Thus, according to the value of α\alpha, we get from (4.5): if α>1\alpha>1, then λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) and σ>1\sigma>1, i.e. u¯a<a\bar{u}_{a}<a and u¯b>b\bar{u}_{b}>b; if α<1\alpha<1, then λ>1\lambda>1 and σ∈(0,1)\sigma\in(0,1), i.e. u¯a>a\bar{u}_{a}>a and u¯b<b\bar{u}_{b}<b; if α=1\alpha=1, then λ=σ=1\lambda=\sigma=1 giving the optimal selection case u¯a=a,u¯b=b\bar{u}_{a}=a,\bar{u}_{b}=b.

Next, let us rewrite the left equation in (4.4) as

σ⁡(1−σ)=ηa​aηb​b​λ​(λ−1)=:K⁡(λ).\sigma(1-\sigma)=\frac{\eta_{a}a}{\eta_{b}b}\lambda(\lambda-1)=:K(\lambda)\,. (4.24)

If α>1\alpha>1, as λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), it follows that K⁡(12)≤K⁡(λ)<0K(\frac{1}{2})\leq K(\lambda)<0 and σ\sigma is upper bounded by the positive root of the above equation with λ=12\lambda=\frac{1}{2}. Hence, (4.22) follows. If α<1\alpha<1, swapping the role between λ\lambda and σ\sigma, we obtain (4.21).

Furthermore, the entries (4.17) of the matrix M⁡(P¯)=M⁡(a​λ+b​σ,0)M(\bar{P})=M(a\lambda+b\sigma,0) are now

M11​(P¯)=ηa​(1−2​λ)​γr+ηb​(1−2​σ)​βr,M12​(P¯)=(ηa​(1−2​λ)−ηb​(1−2​σ))​θr−ηb​σ,M21​(P¯)=0,M22​(P¯)=ηv​(1−σ).\begin{split}M_{11}(\bar{P})&=\eta_{a}(1-2\lambda)\frac{\gamma}{r}+\eta_{b}(1-2\sigma)\frac{\beta}{r}\,,\\ M_{12}(\bar{P})&=\big(\eta_{a}(1-2\lambda)-\eta_{b}(1-2\sigma)\big)\frac{\theta}{r}-\eta_{b}\,\sigma\,,\\ M_{21}(\bar{P})&=0\,,\\ M_{22}(\bar{P})&=\eta_{v}(1-\sigma)\,.\end{split}

As M21=0M_{21}=0, the steady state is linearly stable for the diffusionless macroscopic system if and only if M11<0M_{11}<0 and M22<0M_{22}<0. Hence, σ>1\sigma>1 is a necessary condition for the linear stability, and it holds only if α>1\alpha>1.

In the case α=1\alpha=1, giving the optimal selection case λ=σ=1\lambda=\sigma=1, M⁡(a+b,0)M(a+b,0) has a zero eigenvalue, so that the equilibrium is a non hyperbolic equilibrium. The contribution of the cross-diffusion term does not change the nature of the equilibrium because of the zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian.

Let α>1\alpha>1. The steady states under consideration satisfy Q⁡(λ​a,σ⁡(λ)​b,0)=0Q(\lambda a,\sigma(\lambda)b,0)=0, where σ⁡(λ)\sigma(\lambda) is defined in (4.6). Taking the derivative with respect to λ\lambda and using (4.15), we obtain

Thus

F′​(λ)=ηa​a​(1−2​λ)+ηb​b​σ′​(λ)​(1−2​σ​(λ)),F^{\prime}(\lambda)=\eta_{a}a(1-2\lambda)+\eta_{b}b\,\sigma^{\prime}(\lambda)(1-2\sigma(\lambda))\,, (4.25)

we now find

Hence, M11M_{11} is negative if and only if F′​(λ)F^{\prime}(\lambda) is negative, which implies (i​i)(ii) for the diffusionless macroscopic system and for the cross-diffusion one.

(iii) Let α<1\alpha<1. Since now (λ,σ,δ)=(1,α,1−α)(\lambda,\sigma,\delta)=(1,\alpha,1-\alpha), from (4.17), we have

M⁡(u¯4,v¯4)=−1r​[ηa​γ+ηb​α​βηa​θ+ηb​α​(r−θ)ηv​(1−α)​βηv​(1−α)​(r−θ)].M(\bar{u}_{4},\bar{v}_{4})=-\frac{1}{r}\begin{bmatrix}\eta_{a}\gamma+\eta_{b}\alpha\beta\hskip 9.24994pt&\hskip 9.24994pt\eta_{a}\theta+\eta_{b}\alpha(r-\theta)\\ \eta_{v}(1-\alpha)\beta\hskip 9.24994pt&\hskip 9.24994pt\eta_{v}(1-\alpha)(r-\theta)\end{bmatrix}. (4.26)

tr​M<0.\text{tr}M<0\,. (4.27)

detM=ηv​(1−α)r2​[(ηa​γ+ηb​α​β)​(r−θ)−ηa​θ​β−ηb​α​β​(r−θ)]=ηa​ηv​(1−α)r2​[γ⁡(r−θ)−θ​β]=ηa​ηv​(1−α)r​ϕ1>0,\begin{split}\det M&=\frac{\eta_{v}(1-\alpha)}{r^{2}}\big[(\eta_{a}\gamma+\eta_{b}\alpha\beta)(r-\theta)-\eta_{a}\theta\beta-\eta_{b}\alpha\beta(r-\theta)\big]\\ &=\frac{\eta_{a}\eta_{v}(1-\alpha)}{r^{2}}\big[\gamma(r-\theta)-\theta\beta\big]=\frac{\eta_{a}\eta_{v}(1-\alpha)}{r}\,\phi_{1}>0,\end{split} (4.28)

i.e. the equilibrium (u¯4,v¯4)(\bar{u}_{4},\bar{v}_{4}) is stable for the diffusionless macroscopic system.

The expression form (4.26) for MM implies for NnN_{n}, n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, by (4.19), that

tr ⁡Nn<0,\tr N_{n}<0\,,

and

detNn=A​λn2+B​λn+C,\det{N_{n}}=A\lambda_{n}^{2}+B\lambda_{n}+C\,,

with

4.2 Uniqueness of semi-trivial states with extinction of vv

One possibility to ensure uniqueness of the steady state (u¯3,v¯3)=(a​λ+b​σ,0)(\bar{u}_{3},\bar{v}_{3})=(a\lambda+b\sigma,0) is to impose, in the case α>1\alpha>1, that the net flux of the individuals of the species uu goes from the state ubu_{b} to the state uau_{a}, when the population ubu_{b} reached the capacity of its resource and the population uau_{a} has only halved the capacity of its resource. When α<1\alpha<1, the opposite switching mechanism has to be imposed. A precise version is the following.

Proposition 4.2.

Consider Λ⁡(λ)=λ​ψ​(λ)/ψ1\Lambda(\lambda)=\lambda\psi(\lambda)/\psi_{1} and Σ⁡(σ)=σ​ϕ​(σ)/ϕ1\Sigma(\sigma)=\sigma\phi(\sigma)/\phi_{1}, with ϕ\phi, ψ\psi satisfying assumption (H1). Assume that

α​Λ​(1/2)≤1,ifα>1,\alpha\Lambda(1/2)\leq 1\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{if}\hskip 18.49988pt\alpha>1\,, (4.30)

and

α−1​Σ​(1/2)≤1,ifα<1.\alpha^{-1}\Sigma(1/2)\leq 1\,,\hskip 18.49988pt\text{if}\hskip 18.49988pt\alpha<1\,. (4.31)

Then, there exists a unique solution of (4.4). Furthermore, the corresponding steady state (4.8) is linearly stable if α>1\alpha>1, and unstable if α<1\alpha<1.

Proof.

Let α>1\alpha>1. For the proof recall the function λ↦σ⁡(λ)\lambda\mapsto\sigma(\lambda) from (4.6). Then, σ⁡(0)=0\sigma(0)=0, while the increasing behaviour of Λ\Lambda and Σ\Sigma together with condition (4.30) imply that, for λ∈(0,1/2]\lambda\in(0,1/2],

σ⁡(λ)≤Σ−1​(α​Λ​(1/2))≤Σ−1​(1)=1.\sigma(\lambda)\leq\Sigma^{-1}(\alpha\Lambda(1/2))\leq\Sigma^{-1}(1)=1\,.

Hence, for λ∈(0,1/2]\lambda\in(0,1/2], the function FF from (4.7) is strictly positive.

Now, let λ¯\bar{\lambda} be the smallest zero of FF, so that (a​λ¯+b​σ​(λ¯),0)(a\bar{\lambda}+b\sigma(\bar{\lambda}),0) is one of the steady states under consideration. By the above argument λ¯>1/2\bar{\lambda}>1/2, and by Theorem 4.1, α>1\alpha>1 implies that σ⁡(λ¯)>1\sigma(\bar{\lambda})>1. Therefore, the monotonicity of λ↦σ⁡(λ)\lambda\mapsto\sigma(\lambda) again implies that σ⁡(λ)>1\sigma(\lambda)>1, for any λ≥λ¯\lambda\geq\bar{\lambda}.

Finally, we find from (4.25) that F′​(λ)<0F^{\prime}(\lambda)<0, for all λ≥λ¯\lambda\geq\bar{\lambda}. Hence there exists a unique stationary state and the claimed stability follows from Theorem 4.1.

The case α<1\alpha<1 follows changing the role between the variables λ\lambda and σ\sigma and between the functions Λ\Lambda and Σ\Sigma, i.e. defining λ⁡(σ):=Λ−1​(α−1​Σ​(σ))\lambda(\sigma):=\Lambda^{-1}(\alpha^{-1}\Sigma(\sigma)) and analyzing the behaviour of G⁡(σ):=ηa​a​λ​(σ)​(1−λ⁡(σ))+ηb​b​σ​(1−σ)G(\sigma):=\eta_{a}a\lambda(\sigma)(1-\lambda(\sigma))+\eta_{b}b\sigma(1-\sigma), instead of F⁡(λ)F(\lambda). The claimed instability follows again by Theorem 4.1. ∎

Conditions (4.30) and (4.31) can be rephrased in terms of the ratio ba\frac{b}{a}, respectively as

12​ψ​(12)ϕ1≤ba<ψ1ϕ1andψ1ϕ1<ba≤ψ112​ϕ​(12).\frac{\frac{1}{2}\psi(\frac{1}{2})}{\phi_{1}}\leq\frac{b}{a}<\frac{\psi_{1}}{\phi_{1}}\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988pt\frac{\psi_{1}}{\phi_{1}}<\frac{b}{a}\leq\frac{\psi_{1}}{\frac{1}{2}\phi(\frac{1}{2})}\,.

They are not necessary conditions. Indeed, we provide below a family of conversion rates ψ,ϕ,\psi,\phi, for which the uniqueness of the stationary states (4.8) holds true, whatever is ba\frac{b}{a}. For that family of conversion rates, some numerical test are shown in Section 5.

Since the population densities uau_{a} and ubu_{b} are of the same species, it is natural to expect that the conversion dynamics from uau_{a} to ubu_{b} is similar to that from ubu_{b} to uau_{a}. So, in order to be consistent with the modelling considerations in Subsection 1.2, (see (1.15)), we choose

ψ⁡(x)=ω1​ϕ​(ω2​x),ω1>0,ω2≥0,\psi(x)=\omega_{1}\phi(\omega_{2}x),\hskip 18.49988pt\omega_{1}>0\,,\omega_{2}\geq 0\,, (4.32)

and we prove the following.

Proposition 4.3.

Consider ψ\psi as in (4.32) and

4.3 Linear stability analysis for the mesoscopic system

A triple (u¯aε,u¯bε,v¯ε)(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}) is a homogeneous stationary solutions of the mesoscopic scale problem (1.1) if and only if

fa​(u¯aε)+1ε​Q​(u¯aε,u¯bε,v¯ε)=fb​(u¯bε,v¯ε)−1ε​Q​(u¯aε,u¯bε,v¯ε)=fv​(u¯bε,v¯ε)=0.f_{a}(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon})+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}Q(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=f_{b}(\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}Q(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=f_{v}(\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=0.

If v¯ε=0\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}=0, then either u¯aε=u¯bε=0\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}=\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}=0, which gives the totally trivial steady state corresponding to the trivial macroscopic one (u¯1,v¯1)(\bar{u}_{1},\bar{v}_{1}), or u¯aε≠0\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}\neq 0 and u¯bε≠0\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}\neq 0. In the second case the triplet (u¯aε,u¯bε,0)(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},0) satisfies the system

{ηa​u¯aε​(1−u¯aεa)+1ε​[ϕ⁡(u¯bεb)​u¯bε−ψ⁡(u¯aεa)​u¯aε]=0,ηb​u¯bε​(1−u¯bεb)−1ε​[ϕ⁡(u¯bεb)​u¯bε−ψ⁡(u¯aεa)​u¯aε]=0,\left\{\begin{split}&\eta_{a}\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}(1-\dfrac{\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}}{a})+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\big[\phi(\dfrac{\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}}{b})\,\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}-\psi(\dfrac{\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}}{a})\,\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}\big]=0,\\ &\eta_{b}\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}(1-\dfrac{\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}}{b})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\big[\phi(\dfrac{\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}}{b})\,\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}-\psi(\dfrac{\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}}{a})\,\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon}\big]=0,\end{split}\right.

it can be non unique, as in the macroscopic case, and it converges to a macroscopic equilibrium (u¯3,v¯3)(\bar{u}_{3},\bar{v}_{3}), in the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

If v¯ε≠0\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}\neq 0, then from fv​(ub,v)=0f_{v}(u_{b},v)=0 we have u¯bε+v¯ε=b\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon}+\bar{v}^{\varepsilon}=b. Hence, for all ε>0\varepsilon>0, fb​(u¯bε,v¯ε)=Q⁡(u¯aε,u¯bε,v¯ε)=0f_{b}(\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=Q(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=0 and we obtain the two stationary states (u¯aε,u¯bε,v¯ε)=(0,0,b)(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=(0,0,b) and

(u¯aε,u¯bε,v¯ε)=(a,b​α,b⁡(1−α)),(\bar{u}_{a}^{\varepsilon},\bar{u}_{b}^{\varepsilon},\bar{v}^{\varepsilon})=(a,b\alpha,b(1-\alpha))\,, (4.36)

provided that α<1\alpha<1. These equilibria do not depend on ε>0\varepsilon>0, so that we shall drop the ε\varepsilon exponent in the sequel. In the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, they correspond to the linearly unstable equilibrium (u¯2,v¯2)(\bar{u}_{2},\bar{v}_{2}) and to the positive linearly stable equilibrium (u¯4,v¯4)(\bar{u}_{4},\bar{v}_{4}), respectively.

6 Concluding remarks and discussion

In this paper we derive a (macroscopic) reaction-cross-diffusion system with no flux boundary conditions for two species uu and vv in competition for resources, from a (mesoscopic) diffusion system with slow and fast reaction terms and homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. At the mesoscopic scale, the fast reaction term governs the switching of the individuals of two sub-populations uau_{a} and ubu_{b} of the species uu, into each other, a strategy to optimise the two available ressources consumed by uu. The individuals of the species vv follow a monodiet and evolve competing solely with ubu_{b}. As a consequence, no cross-diffusion term appears in the macroscopic equation for vv. In other words, the reaction-cross-diffusion system is triangular.

Examples of cross-diffusion systems (triangular and not) derived by taking a fast-reaction limit can be found in [10, 15, 5, 6, 12, 14, 21, 2]. A different but equally popular approach for the derivation of cross-diffusion systems (not pursued in this paper) is the mean-field limit of interacting particles, e.g. [17, 11, 4, 16].

For the mathematical analysis, a cross-diffusion term can break general parabolic estimates including the maximum principle, so only local existence results are usually obtained [1]. For global existence, one needs for instance an entropy functional to get a priori estimates and construct a weak solution [14, 21, 16]. Uniqueness is a major problem as well. The key mathematical contribution of this paper is the identification of the entropy functional (1.10), which behaves well under diffusion and the fast-reaction term (1.5). By the obtained control, we are able to undergo the fast reaction limit, to identify the limit densities uu and vv and prove along this way that (u,v)(u,v) is a global in time weak solution. Further studies for the regularity and uniqueness of the solution of a larger class of triangular cross-diffusion systems, including (1.6), are the objects of future works.

An interesting mathematical issue left open in this paper is the discrepancy between the boundary conditions for the mesoscopic and macroscopic systems: for the mesoscopic system (1.1), the no-flux and the Neumann boundary conditions are equivalent, but for the limit system (1.6) we naturally obtain no-flux boundary conditions (1.9). Formally, the no-flux boundary conditions (1.9) are

[da+(db−da)∂1ub∗]∇u⋅σ+[(db−da)∂2ub∗]∇v⋅σ=0and∇v⋅σ=0,\big[d_{a}+(d_{b}-d_{a})\partial_{1}u_{b}^{*}\big]\,\nabla u\cdot\sigma+\big[(d_{b}-d_{a})\partial_{2}u_{b}^{*}\big]\,\nabla v\cdot\sigma=0\hskip 18.49988pt\text{and}\hskip 18.49988pt\nabla v\cdot\sigma=0,

where ub∗=ub∗​(u,v)u_{b}^{*}=u_{b}^{*}(u,v) is the unique solution to (1.7) for given uu and vv. Differentiating the condition Q⁡(u−ub∗​(u,v),ub∗​(u,v),v)=0Q(u-u_{b}^{*}(u,v),u_{b}^{*}(u,v),v)=0 with respect to uu yields

∂1ub∗=ψ⁡(u−ub∗a)+u−ub∗a​ψ′​(u−ub∗a)ϕ⁡(ub∗+vb)+ub∗b​ϕ′​(ub∗+vb)+ψ⁡(u−ub∗a)+u−ub∗a​ψ′​(u−ub∗a).\partial_{1}u_{b}^{*}=\frac{\psi\Big(\frac{u-u_{b}^{*}}{a}\Big)+\frac{u-u_{b}^{*}}{a}\psi^{\prime}\Big(\frac{u-u_{b}^{*}}{a}\Big)}{\phi\Big(\frac{u_{b}^{*}+v}{b}\Big)+\frac{u_{b}^{*}}{b}\phi^{\prime}\Big(\frac{u_{b}^{*}+v}{b}\Big)+\psi\Big(\frac{u-u_{b}^{*}}{a}\Big)+\frac{u-u_{b}^{*}}{a}\psi^{\prime}\Big(\frac{u-u_{b}^{*}}{a}\Big)}.

Hence by our assumptions ∂1ub∗∈(0,1)\partial_{1}u_{b}^{*}\in(0,1), which implies [da+(db−da)​∂1ub∗]>0\big[d_{a}+(d_{b}-d_{a})\partial_{1}u_{b}^{*}\big]>0. Therefore, the no-flux boundary condition is formally equivalent to the Neumann boundary condition. It would be interesting to see whether singularities can break this equivalence.

From a modelling point of view, we show that the competition between uu and vv described above, can be modelled by a Lotka-Volterra competitive type system, with competitive coefficients derived by the population dynamics. To the best of the author’s knowledge, the meaning of the classical Lotka-Volterra competition system is only abstract, and connecting the system coefficients to specific situations is rarely been done. We are able to answer to this fundamental question in the specific model of the paper. Indeed, dropping the diffusion terms, the competition system (1.6)–(1.7) reads as

{∂tu=ηa​ua​(1−uaa)+ηb​ub​(1−ub+vb),∂tv=ηv​v​(1−ub+vb),\left\{\begin{aligned} \partial_{t}u&=\eta_{a}u_{a}\left(1-\dfrac{u_{a}}{a}\right)+\eta_{b}u_{b}\left(1-\dfrac{u_{b}+v}{b}\right),\\ \partial_{t}v&=\eta_{v}v\left(1-\dfrac{u_{b}+v}{b}\right),\end{aligned}\right. (6.1)

and

u=ua+ub,ϕ⁡(ub+vb)​ub=ψ⁡(uaa)​ua.u=u_{a}+u_{b},\hskip 9.24994pt\phi\Big(\frac{u_{b}+v}{b}\Big)u_{b}=\psi\Big(\frac{u_{a}}{a}\Big)u_{a}\,. (6.2)

Let

ra​(ua,ub,v):=(1+ψ⁡(uaa)ϕ⁡(ub+vb))−1​ and ​rb​(ua,ub,v):=(1+ϕ⁡(ub+vb)ψ⁡(uaa))−1.r_{a}(u_{a},u_{b},v):=\left(1+\frac{\psi(\frac{u_{a}}{a})}{\phi(\frac{u_{b}+v}{b})}\right)^{-1}\ \text{ and }\ \ r_{b}(u_{a},u_{b},v):=\left(1+\frac{\phi(\frac{u_{b}+v}{b})}{\psi(\frac{u_{a}}{a})}\right)^{-1}. (6.3)

Then, it holds

ua=ra​u,ub=rb​u,ra+rb=1,0<ra,rb<1,u_{a}=r_{a}u,\hskip 9.24994ptu_{b}=r_{b}u,\hskip 9.24994ptr_{a}+r_{b}=1,\hskip 9.24994pt0<r_{a},r_{b}<1,

and the system can be rewritten in terms of uu and vv, as the following Lotka-Volterra system

{ut=ηu​(1−b11​u−b12​v)​u,vt=ηv​(1−b21​u−b22​v)​v,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\eta_{u}(1-b_{11}u-b_{12}v)u,&\\ v_{t}=\eta_{v}(1-b_{21}u-b_{22}v)v,&\end{cases} (6.4)

where the competition coefficients are given by

b11=ηa​ra2/a+ηb​rb2/bηa​ra+ηb​rb,b12=ηb​rb/bηa​ra+ηb​rb,b21=rbb,b22=1b,b_{11}=\frac{\eta_{a}r_{a}^{2}/a+\eta_{b}r_{b}^{2}/b}{\eta_{a}r_{a}+\eta_{b}r_{b}},\hskip 9.24994ptb_{12}=\frac{\eta_{b}r_{b}/b}{\eta_{a}r_{a}+\eta_{b}r_{b}},\hskip 9.24994ptb_{21}=\frac{r_{b}}{b},\hskip 9.24994ptb_{22}=\frac{1}{b}, (6.5)

and the growth rates are

ηu=ηa​ra+ηb​rb and ηv.\eta_{u}=\eta_{a}r_{a}+\eta_{b}r_{b}\hskip 18.49988pt\text{ and }\hskip 18.49988pt\eta_{v}\,. (6.6)

The fundamental difference between the classical Lotka-Volterra competition system and our model (6.4)-(6.6) is in the solution dependency of the coefficients rar_{a} and rbr_{b} in (6.3) and thus of the bi​jb_{ij}’s. Our understanding is that the classical Lotka-Volterra competition system with constant coefficients bi​jb_{ij} should be considered locally, where the coefficients variation is small, while (6.4)-(6.6), can be considered globally. In this viewpoint, we can still call the competition modelled by system (6.4)-(6.6) a strong competition if b12/b11>1b_{12}/b_{11}>1 and b21/b22>1b_{21}/b_{22}>1 for all solutions.

A systematic study on the derivation of advection and cross-diffusion terms from a given population dynamics with meaningful parameter regimes is performed in [9, Section 4].

Again from a modelling perspective, a motivation to consider reaction-cross-diffusion systems is the possibility to find instabilities due to the cross-diffusion, where a normal diffusion cannot induce instabilities. The identification of these cross-diffusion induced instabilities is a very active research area [20, 31, 3]. This has been the motivation of our investigation of spatially homogeneous stationary states and their linear stability in Section 4. For semi-trivial stationary states with v=0v=0, we see that the fast-reaction term can lead to non-trivial behaviour (lack of uniqueness), see also [23]. On the other hand, the totally non-trivial homogeneous steady state (coexistence state) is unique and linearly stable. Thus, the possibility of cross-diffusion induced instability is ruled out in that case.

The existence of heterogeneous steady states of the macroscopic system is not discarded, and it will be analyzed in a forthcoming paper.

and where [Mε]i​i[M^{\varepsilon}]_{ii} are the following minors:

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
